messages.author: d3f79de273e1d348
messages.subject: Using a MCDS (with species as covariate) to run a DSM for an specific species
parts:
Hi all!

Thank you for sharing your knowledge. I need your advice. My study area has 17 ungulate species (from duiker to giraffe), with different number of detections (from 20 to 400 sightings per species). I want to explore the relative effect of environment factors on the spatial abundance of each species using DSMs. I am not interested in predicting abundance. Due to I have less than 40-60 detections for some species, I estimated a global detection function pooling all detections together (around 3000 detections) using ds(). My best function was a hazard-rate with species as a covariate (17 levels).

Now I want to build species specific DSMs including the previous detection function, but I am not sure this recognised I am only assessing an specific species. From a previous post (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/distance-sampling/detection$20function$20covariate%7Csort:date/distance-sampling/vYc5CzfM86Y/7AaDGPycAwAJ), people talked it is necessary to estimate the "deflection effect": the amount by which the shape of the rare species is deflected from the shape of the common species.

Does DSMs does that (fix the detection function to the species that are included) by itself?
If it doesnt...How can I calculate and include the deflection effect in my DSMs in order to fix the detection function for each species?
Is it better to estimate a global detection function for only the most similar species?. (for example do not include giraffe and duiker sightings in same detection functions)

thank you so much!!!
have a nice day
regards
nicolas

messages.author: 9dce01a6123da978
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Using a MCDS (with species as covariate) to run a DSM for an specific species
parts:
Hi Nicolás,

Just a wee warning - if your main interest is in looking at the effect of various environmental factors on relative abundance of different species, and you have used a global detection function over all species, you might need to keep an eye on whether any of your environmental factors (e.g. along the lines of habitat type, tree density, ground vegetation height etc.) might have species-specific effects on detectability. For example, tall grass might not affect detectability of giraffe, but probably would affect that of a small animal like duiker. If this is the case, you might be better off opting for several detection functions, with species you would expect to share similar patterns in detectability (i.e. in response to the relevant environmental variation) grouped together. You might also need to have one or more environmental variables included in your detection function.

I think this is more or less what you are suggesting in your last question. Anyway, with regard to exactly how to specify the relevant models, and including 'deflection effects', others on this forum will likely be much better able to advise than I can. But your instinct that detection functions including both giraffe and duiker registrations may cause problems is probably a good one!

Cheers,

Mark

messages.author: 350dad0a615d36db
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Using a MCDS (with species as covariate) to run a DSM for an specific species
parts:
Hi listfolk,

Just reporting back after a wee off-list chat with Nicolás about this.

Bearing in mind Mark Wilson's advice earlier in the thread, from a
coding perspective, dsm makes this simple. All you need to do is subset
your observation data.frame correctly and dsm() will pick out the
correct data.

So, say you have your observation frame, called obsdata and it has a
column called "species" which has which species your observation is
from. Let's say you are interested in the species "babelfish", you can
then do

obsdata_babel <- subset(obsdata, species=="babelfish")

then feed this to dsm() with the full segment data and the detection
function that has species as a covariate in it.

The DSM will then be fitted using only the babelfish observations.


cheers,
--dave
